learn.hook: Living under one roof for years and still talking like strangers: many families know that silence. Elizabeth Jennings puts it into a father's voice.
points: Elizabeth Jennings was an English poet; in 'Father to Son' the speaker is a father talking about his grown son.
Form: four stanzas of six lines each; each stanza follows the same rhyme pattern (abbaba), though many rhymes are only half-rhymes (child/build/killed).
The father says he does not understand his son, even though they have lived together in the same house for years.
He admits he knows nothing of him and tries to build a relationship from memories of how the son was when small.
They speak like strangers; there is no sign of understanding between them.

example.q: Who is the speaker, and what is his problem?
steps: The speaker is a father.
He has lived with his son for years.
Yet he cannot understand him; they talk like strangers.
example.answer: A father who, despite years in the same house, cannot understand or connect with his grown son.

learn.reallife: In many Indian homes, parents and teens spend hours under one roof yet talk little beyond 'Have you eaten?'. The poem captures that gap.

topics.title: Seed, land and what the son loves

learn.hook: A father who planted a seed, only to find the land it grew on now belongs to someone else. Jennings packs a generation gap into one farming metaphor.
points: The father wonders if he has wasted the 'seed' he spent, or sown it in land that is the son's and not his.
Metaphors: 'seed' = his child, the effort and love he invested; 'land' = the son's own world, which the father cannot enter.
The son is 'built to my design' (like the father), yet what the son loves, the father cannot share.
Silence surrounds them; neither can reach the other.
Lines showing their difference: 'what he loves I cannot share'; 'we speak like strangers'; the son making and moving his own world.

example.q: Explain the metaphor of the seed and the land.
steps: Seed: the son, and the love and effort the father put into him.
Land: the son's own life and world.
The father fears his seed grew in land that is no longer his.
example.answer: The father invested himself in his son, but the son has grown into his own world, outside the father's reach.

learn.reallife: Indian parents often say 'we sowed, now you reap'. In the poem the harvest grows in a field the father can no longer enter.

topics.title: The prodigal son and anger from grief

learn.hook: In a famous Bible parable, a son who wasted everything comes home and is welcomed with a feast. The father in this poem almost wishes for that story.
points: The father would rather have his son prodigal, returning to his father's house, the home he knew, than see him make and move his own world.
Biblical allusion: the parable of the prodigal son, who leaves, wastes his inheritance and returns home to be forgiven by his father.
The father says he would forgive him too, shaping a new love out of sorrow.
Father and son must live on the same globe and the same land: they cannot escape each other.
Paradox: the father cannot understand why anger grows from grief; sorrow at the distance turns into anger.

example.q: What is the allusion to the prodigal son, and why is it used?
steps: Parable: a son leaves, wastes his inheritance, returns, and is forgiven.
The father wishes his son would 'return' like that.
It shows his longing to forgive and reconnect.
example.answer: It refers to the Bible's prodigal son; the father wishes his son would come back so he could forgive him and love him anew.

learn.reallife: In many Indian families, a child who moves to another city and stops calling is welcomed back with open arms on Diwali. That is the 'prodigal' longing.

topics.title: An empty hand: helplessness and hope

learn.hook: Two people, each holding out an empty hand, each waiting for the other to make the first move. The poem ends right there.
points: Ending: father and son each put out an empty hand, longing for something to forgive.
'Empty hand' (metaphor): an offer of peace with nothing yet to give, and a sign of helplessness.
The father's helplessness: he cannot understand, cannot share, cannot even explain his own anger; he can only wish and wait.
He also shows possessiveness (wanting the son back in his house) and a longing for reconciliation.
Rhyme and repetition: each stanza follows the same abbaba pattern, but with many half-rhymes; the repeated word 'understand' stresses the gap; imagery of silence fills the poem.

example.q: How is the father's helplessness shown?
steps: He says he does not understand his son.
He cannot share what the son loves.
He cannot understand his own anger; he can only hold out an empty hand.
example.answer: Through his repeated failure to understand, his inability to share and his empty, waiting hand.

learn.reallife: Family counsellors in Indian cities often say the first step is just reaching out, even when you have no perfect words. The empty hand is that first step.

learn.hook: The poem never names the father or son, their country or their quarrel. That silence makes it everyone's story.
points: Theme: the generation gap and the lack of communication between parent and child.
Family misunderstanding is universal: it happens across cultures and times.
Personal or universal? Spoken as one father's experience, but with no names or specific details, so it reads as universal.
Exam focus: extract questions on metaphors (seed, land, empty hand), allusion, paradox and tone; short answers on the generation gap.

example.q: Is the poem about a personal or a universal experience?
steps: It is spoken by one father in the first person.
It has no names, places or specific quarrels.
Many families feel the same gap.
example.answer: Though personal in voice, it describes a universal experience of parents and children growing apart.

learn.reallife: From joint families in Kolkata to nuclear families in Bengaluru, parents and teens everywhere argue about careers, phones and friends: a universal gap.
